summary: This Best Current Practice describes threats against cross-device flows, such as logging in on a TV using a phone, along with mitigations, protocol selection guidance, and a summary of relevant formal analysis. It serves system designers and engineers.

plainLanguage.summary: When you use your phone to sign in on another gadget, someone might trick you. This lists the tricks and how to stop them.

questions: is the oauth device authorization grant safe
subtitle: How attackers trick people into approving logins on a phone for the attacker's TV or laptop, and how to defend against it.

tldr.problem: In cross-device flows, such as scanning a QR code on a TV with a phone, the link between the two devices is unauthenticated, so attackers can use phishing-style tricks to get users to authorize the attacker's device or hand over codes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes three authorization patterns and one session transfer pattern, shows how each is attacked, and lists 17 practical mitigations, guidance on choosing between the device authorization grant, CIBA and FIDO2/WebAuthn, and results of formal analysis.
tldr.outcome: Implementers must do a risk assessment and pick mitigations, should avoid cross-device flows if the risks cannot be reduced, and should prefer FIDO cross-device authentication where devices allow it.

today: RFC 10027 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 247) published in August 2026, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It gives guidance for the device authorization grant in RFC 8628 and similar flows.

sections.title: The Cross-Device Problem
sections.content:
A cross-device flow spans more than one of a person's devices. A common example is scanning a QR code shown on a smart TV with a phone so that a TV app can reach a streaming account. Other versions use a PIN typed on one device or a push notification approved on another.

In every case the user decides whether to grant authorization, but the QR code or PIN travels over an unauthenticated channel, so the user has to judge the context. Attackers exploit that. The RFC splits the topic in two: cross-device authorization, where a second, personally trusted device (the Authorization Device) authorizes the first (the Consumption Device), and cross-device session transfer, where an already authenticated session moves to a second device.

Attacks on the first kind are called Cross-Device Consent Phishing (CDCP), and on the second kind Cross-Device Session Phishing (CDSP). They do not harvest passwords. They persuade the user to grant authorization, so they work even when multi-factor authentication is used. Once the attacker has access and refresh tokens, they can attempt lateral attacks or sell the tokens.
sections.plainLanguage: When you use your phone to approve a login on your TV, nothing proves the TV is really yours. A trickster can pretend to be your TV, and you have to be the one who notices.

sections.title: The Best Practices
sections.content:
The OAuth Working Group lists five practices. Implementers MUST perform a risk assessment weighing CDCP and CDSP risks against the benefits for users. They SHOULD avoid cross-device flows if risks cannot be sufficiently mitigated, and SHOULD follow the protocol selection guidance. They MUST select appropriate mitigations to address the risks they identified, and SHOULD include proximity among them if possible.

These practices apply to the device authorization grant (RFC 8628) and to other protocols that rely on the user to authenticate the channel between devices, including CIBA, SIOPv2, OpenID for Verifiable Presentations and the Pre-Authorized Code Flow.

Cross-device protocols SHOULD NOT be used when both roles are on the same device. The OAuth authorization code grant from RFC 6749 and OpenID Connect Core fit that case better. A server may try to detect same-device use, but with Network Address Translation many devices can share one address, so inferring this can be wrong.
sections.plainLanguage: Before building a login-by-phone feature, stop and think about how it could be abused. If you cannot make it safe enough, do not build it.

sections.title: Four Flow Patterns
sections.content:
In the User-Transferred Session Data Pattern, the user carries information from the Consumption Device to the Authorization Device by reading a code or scanning a QR code. The device authorization grant (RFC 8628) works this way. The Consumption Device asks the authorization server for a code, shows it, and polls until authorization is granted.

In the Backchannel-Transferred Session Pattern, the client on the Consumption Device asks the authorization server over a backchannel to request authorization on the Authorization Device, for example with a push notification or a text message with a link. CIBA is the example.

In the User-Transferred Authorization Data Pattern, the server sends authorization data, such as a 6-digit code, to the Authorization Device, and the user types it into the Consumption Device. The RFC says the 6-digit length is illustrative.

The Cross-Device Session Transfer Pattern is different. The user is already authenticated on the Authorization Device, requests a session transfer code, often shown as a QR code, and enters or scans it on the Consumption Device, which presents it to the server to receive the session context. The RFC gives nine example scenarios, A1 to A9, from a smart TV and a bike sharing scheme to adding a phone to a corporate network.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four ways a phone and another gadget can team up: you copy a code to the phone, the server pings the phone, the phone shows a number you type into the gadget, or you move your logged-in session across with a code.

sections.title: How the Attacks Work
sections.content:
In all the attacks, the attacker uses social engineering to change the context in which a code or request is shown. The RFC covers only cases where the user is misled, not users who knowingly cooperate with the attacker.

  • Session data pattern: the attacker starts the flow, copies the QR or user code, and sends it to many users with a lure such as a loyalty reward or a warning that files will be deleted within 24 hours. A user who authorizes gives the attacker's device the tokens. Another example copies a bike's QR code onto a label placed on a different bike.
  • Backchannel pattern: the attacker triggers authorization requests without the user's involvement, either in bulk for many users or as a flood timed to wake an administrator, hoping someone approves. A fake help desk call can also prime a user to approve a transfer.
  • Authorization data pattern: the attacker triggers a code to be sent to the user's phone, then calls pretending to be support and asks the user to read it back.
  • Session transfer: the attacker persuades a user to generate a transfer QR code, for example claiming to investigate a breach, and send it over, then scans it to join the network or take over the application session.
sections.plainLanguage: The tricksters start the login on their own device, then talk you into approving it with a fake reward, a scary message or a phone call. Nothing about the phone approval tells you whose login it really is.

sections.title: Practical Mitigations
sections.content:
The RFC recommends applying one or more of its mitigations, since each adds a layer even though none is complete. They aim to prevent an attack from starting, disrupt it in progress, or recover if it succeeds.

  • Establish proximity: physical connection, wireless proximity (NFC, Bluetooth Low Energy, UWB), a shared network or geolocation. Each can be circumvented, for example with a VPN or a spoofed GNSS position.
  • Short-lived, one-time and unique codes: shrink the window and stop one code being sent to many victims.
  • Content filtering of messages carrying codes, and detect and remediate by invalidating tokens, using token introspection or CAEP messages.
  • Trusted devices and trusted networks: only let known devices or networks start a flow.
  • Limited scopes, short-lived tokens and sender-constrained tokens: reduce the damage if the attack succeeds.
  • Rate limits, good user experience (make decline the default or equally prominent) and user education.
  • Authenticate then initiate, request initiation verification with an OTP or PIN, and request binding with out-of-band data.

Each mitigation comes with listed limitations. For example, user education alone is insufficient, and a sophisticated attacker can request the QR code only after the victim clicks a phishing link, defeating short lifetimes.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no single lock. The advice is to stack several small ones: make codes expire fast, check the devices are close together, limit what a stolen pass can do, and make it easy to say no.

sections.title: Choosing a Protocol
sections.content:
The RFC compares three protocols. The device authorization grant assumes nothing about device capabilities, so it works on the widest range of devices, but public reports show it can be abused. Use it only if other protocols are not viable, avoid it for sensitive, high value or business critical resources, and always add mitigations such as proximity or pre-registered devices.

CIBA is less susceptible because the user is contacted by the OpenID Provider rather than scanning a code, but attackers who know or guess a user identifier can still start requests. Use it instead of the device grant when the Consumption Device can obtain a user identifier and the server can trigger authorization on the Authorization Device.

FIDO2/WebAuthn with CTAP 2.2 hybrid transports uses an encrypted Bluetooth Low Energy advertisement after a QR scan, so it proves proximity. It requires BLE and internet access on both devices. The RFC says it SHOULD be used whenever devices can and a suitable FIDO credential is not on the Consumption Device. It can be combined with the authorization code grant and PKCE (RFC 7636) for cross-device authorization without the risks of the device grant.
sections.plainLanguage: Some login methods are like a locked door with a key that only works nearby. The simplest method is like a door anyone can knock on. The RFC says to prefer the nearby-key kind when you can.

sections.title: What Formal Analysis Shows
sections.content:
The RFC explains that formal security analysis uses mathematical models to describe a protocol, its environment and its goals. Its strengths are that it can find attacks nobody thought of and can rule out attacks within the model. Its downside is a gap between model and implementation.

Four works are summarized. A Web Infrastructure Model analysis of SIOPv2 confirmed a request replay attack, and a Cross-Device Stub that links the two devices beforehand was shown effective in the model, which resembles the trusted device relationship in the mitigations. A similar analysis of GNAP found the same attack, and showed a careful user could prevent it in theory. Pernpruner et al. analyzed push-notification approval, identifying "implicit attacks" that match CDCP, and a QR-code-scan protocol, from which they proposed mitigations such as user education, request initiation verification and request binding.
sections.plainLanguage: Researchers draw a protocol as a math puzzle to hunt for tricks, like testing a lock on paper. It finds new problems, but real products can still differ from the paper version.
